name: The Epic of Gilgamesh: The Babylonian Epic Poem and Other Texts in Akkadian and Sumerian (Penguin, trans. Andrew George) and The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic: Introduction, Critical Edition and Cuneiform Texts (Oxford University Press)
date: Translation: 1999 (Allen Lane The Penguin Press hardback; Penguin Classics paperback 2000, ISBN 0140447210; later Penguin Classics printings with revisions [uncertain: exact revised-edition years]). Critical edition: 2003 (Oxford University Press, two volumes, nearly 1,000 pages). Score transliterations of individual Standard Babylonian tablets made open access via SOAS Research Online and listed in UCF STARS 'Open Educational Resources for the Ancient Near East' (available from 28 August 2020)
creator: Andrew R. George (b. 1955), British Assyriologist, Professor of Babylonian at SOAS, University of London; PhD under W. G. Lambert (1985). Publishers: Penguin (translation) and Oxford University Press (critical edition)
form: Two linked works. (1) Penguin: verse translation, one English line per cuneiform line, of the Standard Babylonian epic in twelve tablets plus separate translations of the Old Babylonian and Middle Babylonian fragments and the five Sumerian Bilgames poems, with introduction, notes and glossary. (2) OUP: critical edition, a composite variorum text in transliteration with a score of every manuscript, cuneiform hand-copies, philological commentary and a literal English translation
translator_access: Direct and first-hand. George reads Akkadian and Sumerian and established the text himself by collating the tablets in the British Museum and other collections, making new hand-copies. The Penguin translation was produced alongside the critical edition, so it is the reading-text of the same scholar who built the underlying edition. No crib involved
scholarly_adviser: N/A: George is the specialist. He is the adviser others lean on (later poet-translators and teachers cite his edition as their base text)
versions_used: Standard Babylonian (the eleven-tablet 'Sîn-lēqi-unninni' version) plus Tablet XII as the core text; Old Babylonian tablets (Pennsylvania, Yale, Sippar/Meissner and others) and Middle Babylonian peripheral fragments (Megiddo, Emar, Ugarit, Hattusa) translated separately; the five Sumerian Bilgames poems (Bilgames and Akka, Bilgames and Huwawa, Bull of Heaven, Death of Bilgames, Bilgames and the Netherworld). The Sulaymaniyah Tablet V fragment postdates both books; George published it with Farouk Al-Rawi in 2014 ('Back to the Cedar Forest', Journal of Cuneiform Studies 66)
non_standard_material: Kept apart rather than merged. The Penguin volume prints the Standard Babylonian epic first, then the older Akkadian and Sumerian texts as separate sections, so the reader can compare them rather than read a blended story. Where the Standard text is lost and George supplies an episode from another source, the switch is announced with a note naming the source tablet [uncertain: exact typographic convention used for these inserts, e.g. italic headings versus marginal notes]
gap_policy: Shown. George's stated aim is to indicate every lacuna so readers know what is established and what is surmised (Penguin blurb; Literary Review, 1999). Missing lines are marked and often counted, restorations are flagged, and nothing is invented to make the story run smoothly. The critical edition goes further, printing the damage of each manuscript line by line
typography_of_absence: Square brackets for restored words; ellipses for unrecoverable text; italics for doubtful or uncertain renderings; editorial notes stating how many lines are lost where a column breaks off [uncertain: exact mapping of italics versus brackets in each printing]. The result is a page visibly punctured by gaps. The Literary Review found the effect 'not always an entirely fluent read'
tablet_xii: Included, as the twelfth tablet after the Tablet XI ending, and discussed in the introduction as an appended Akkadian translation of the second half of the Sumerian 'Bilgames and the Netherworld', not an organic continuation. George suggests it was attached because it complements the epic's concern with death. Readers therefore meet two endings: the walls of Uruk (XI) and Enkidu's report from the underworld (XII)
turning_point: The death of Enkidu (Tablets VII to VIII) is the hinge, and George's apparatus makes the shape clearer than most versions because it separates Standard Babylonian from Old Babylonian. In the Standard text Siduri is a gatekeeper; her famous 'let your belly be full' advice survives only in the Old Babylonian Sippar tablet, which George translates in its own section. So in his main text the lesson falls to Uta-napishti's speech on death and the failed sleep test in Tablet XI, and the story resolves at the walls of Uruk. His reading of the first line ('He who saw the Deep', the Apsû, instead of the older 'He who saw everything') also moves the weight toward wisdom brought back from the edge of the world
arc_interpretation: Wisdom through failure, framed by kingship. George's introduction presents the epic as the story of a king who seeks immortality, fails, and returns with knowledge that makes him a better ruler and a mortal man at peace with that. Evidence: the prologue promises one who 'saw the Deep' and 'brought back a message from before the Flood'; the narrative ends not with the lost plant but with Gilgamesh showing Ur-shanabi the city he built; the Old Babylonian incipit 'Surpassing all other kings' stresses royal identity. The grief over Enkidu drives the quest, but the outcome George emphasises is acceptance and legacy (the wall and the written record) rather than despair
key_passages: Shamhat and Enkidu (Tablet I): Shamhat 'unfastened the cloth of her loins, she bared her sex and he took in her charms', then 'for six days and seven nights Enkidu was erect, as he coupled with Shamhat' [uncertain: exact wording]. Direct, with 'harlot' largely avoided in favour of her name. Siduri (Old Babylonian Sippar tablet, printed separately): 'The life that you seek you never will find: when the gods created mankind, death they dispensed to mankind, life they kept for themselves. But you, Gilgamesh, let your belly be full, enjoy yourself always by day and by night!' [uncertain: exact wording]. Death in the bedchamber (Tablet XI): 'in my bed-chamber Death does abide, and wherever I turn, there too will be Death' [uncertain: exact wording]. Walls of Uruk (Tablet XI): 'O Ur-shanabi, climb Uruk's wall and walk back and forth! Survey its foundations, examine the brickwork! Were its bricks not fired in an oven? Did the Seven Sages not lay its foundations? A square mile is city, a square mile date-grove, a square mile is clay-pit, half a square mile the temple of Ishtar: three square miles and a half is Uruk's expanse' [uncertain: exact wording]. Units converted into modern measures instead of leagues
diction_and_metre: Loose, stress-based lines that follow the Akkadian couplet structure (each line tends to fall into two halves, echoing the caesura of Babylonian verse). Plain modern British English with a slightly formal, elevated register; no archaism, occasional inversions to keep the rhythm ('death they dispensed to mankind'). Repetitions and formulaic lines kept as in the original. Alan Wall found the rhythm could induce 'narcosis when persisted in for too long' (Literary Review, February 1999)
sample_line: "He who saw the Deep, the country's foundation, [who] knew ..., was wise in all matters!" (Tablet I, lines 1-2, George, Penguin 1999) [uncertain: exact punctuation]
critical_response: Quickly became the scholarly standard in English, displacing Sandars in Penguin Classics and superseding Kovacs for accuracy. Alan Wall (Literary Review, issue 248, February 1999) called it 'very impressive' and 'invaluable as a convenient guide to all the different strands', praising an introduction of 'scholarship and lucidity' but judging the text not always fluent and short on the 'verve, rhythm and lexical inventiveness' of great epic translations. The 2003 OUP edition is widely treated as the definitive edition of the Standard Babylonian text and the base for later translations and teaching [uncertain: specific named academic reviews]
controversies: Little dispute over accuracy. The recurring debate is literary: whether a gap-marked scholarly version can compete as poetry with freer versions (Mitchell 2004, Ferry 1992), and George's pointed remarks about 'versions' by non-specialists feed that argument [uncertain: specific published exchange]. The critical edition's composite text also means readers see a reconstruction, not any single ancient manuscript, which is standard practice but occasionally questioned. Later finds (Sulaymaniyah tablet, fragments identified by the Electronic Babylonian Library) mean parts of the 2003 edition are now superseded, which George himself documents
regional_reception: George's link to the region runs through collaboration more than translation: the 2014 publication of the Sulaymaniyah Museum's Tablet V fragment with Iraqi scholar Farouk Al-Rawi, of an object held in Iraqi Kurdistan. The Penguin has been translated or used as a base for versions in other languages [uncertain: specific Arabic or Kurdish editions]. The open-access score transliterations make the edition freely usable by scholars in Iraq and elsewhere without buying the OUP volumes
ai_craft_tension: George's critical edition is the human groundwork that machine projects now build on. His score transliterations (every manuscript lined up sign by sign) are exactly the structured data that fragment-matching tools such as the Electronic Babylonian Library use to find new joins, and their open release in 2020 made that easier. What a machine cannot yet supply is the judgement in the Penguin: deciding which ancient version to print, where a restoration is safe, and how to render a Babylonian couplet in readable English while leaving the holes visible. George's refusal to smooth gaps is itself a choice a model trained to produce fluent text would tend to erase. His work also shows an edition is never finished: the Sulaymaniyah tablet arrived eleven years after the OUP volumes
essay_hooks: (1) First line reinterpreted: 'He who saw the Deep' instead of 'He who saw everything', one word changing the hero from all-knowing to someone who reached the cosmic waters. (2) Siduri's famous carpe diem speech is not in the Standard Babylonian epic at all; George prints it separately from an Old Babylonian tablet, so a faithful reader sees it as a lost draft. (3) Nearly 1,000 pages of critical edition behind a slim Penguin paperback. (4) Literary Review (1999): 'not always an entirely fluent read', a fair price for honesty about gaps. (5) Score transliterations open access since August 2020 (UCF STARS, SOAS Research Online): the data layer machines now mine for fragment matches. (6) Uruk measured in 'square miles' rather than leagues, a small translator's decision that makes the ending land for a modern reader. (7) Eleven years after the 'definitive' edition, a tablet in Sulaymaniyah added some 20 lines to Tablet V (Al-Rawi and George 2014) [uncertain: line count]
